The Great skua (Stercorarius skua) is a large, predatory seabird that breeds across the North Atlantic, with key populations in Scotland, Iceland, and Norway. Field studies of this species have documented that newly hatched chicks emerge from the egg at a modest body mass, typically weighing around 72 grams [Wwb = around 72 grams]. This neonatal weight, recorded during systematic nest-monitoring programs, is relatively high among charadriiform seabirds, reflecting the substantial yolk reserves that support early development within the egg. The fledging period, a critical transition when young birds achieve their first sustained flight and begin to gain independence from parental care, is estimated at 45 days after hatching [tx = 45 days after hatching] under natural conditions at a temperature of 40.9 °C [T = 40.9 °C]. This relatively rapid development to fledging is made possible by the high rates of food provisioning that both parents supply, allowing the nestling to attain the requisite wing and muscle maturation quickly. In comparison to smaller congeners like the Arctic skua, the Great skua's larger body size is associated with a slightly extended nestling period, though the difference remains modest given the pronounced size disparity. The thermal environment of the nest site, particularly during the off-duty periods when an adult leaves to forage, can influence growth rates, but the core developmental schedule is remarkably consistent across the breeding range.

Sexual maturation in this species is not achieved quickly; rather, it unfolds over a considerably longer timeframe than the initial growth to fledging. The onset of puberty, marking the achievement of reproductive capacity, is reached at approximately 135 days since birth [tp = approximately 135 days since birth] at a temperature of 40.9 °C [T = 40.9 °C]. This period of adolescence, which extends well beyond the fledging event, involves the continued refinement of foraging skills and the accumulation of body stores necessary to support the energetic demands of future reproduction. During this subadult phase, young birds often remain in the vicinity of the breeding colony but do not participate in breeding activities, instead engaging in social displays and honing their hunting techniques. The relatively late onset of puberty, compared to the timing of fledging, indicates a life-history strategy where somatic development and behavioral competence are prioritized before any investment in gamete production begins. Individuals that delay maturation may be better equipped to compete for high-quality territories and mates upon reaching adulthood. Available data from long-term banding studies on Foula and St Kilda suggest that this 135-day period (135 days since birth) [tp = 135 days since birth] is a robust estimate for the transition from fully dependent juvenile to a physiologically mature, though not yet breeding, bird at a temperature of 40.9 °C [T = 40.9 °C].

First reproduction in Great skua is deferred substantially beyond the point of sexual maturity, reflecting the intense competition for nest sites and the high costs of parental care in this aggressive, long-lived species. The age at which an individual produces its first brood is typically 2190 days since birth [tR = 2190 days since birth], a figure derived from decades of mark-recapture data on the Shetland archipelago at a temperature of 40.9 °C [T = 40.9 °C]. This delay of several years, which translates into an age of about six years before a bird first lays eggs, is a classic feature of a slow life history, where initial reproductive bouts are postponed in favor of maximizing adult survival and breeding-site tenure. The extended pre-breeding period allows young adults to acquire experience, secure a territory, and form a durable pair bond with a partner, all of which are prerequisites for successful fledging. In terms of total lifetime, the oldest documented Great skua individuals have been recorded living for approximately 16 years [am = approximately 16 years] in the wild, a longevity that places it among the more long- at a temperature of 40.9 °C [T = 40.9 °C]lived seabirds. This impressive lifespan, confirmed by ring recoveries from the BTO ringing scheme, underscores the species' capacity for repeated reproductive output across many breeding seasons. During this extended adult life, birds produce only one brood per year typically.

Under the thermal conditions typical of active metabolic periods (40.9 °C [T = 40.9 °C]), reproductive output in the Great skua is tightly constrained by the harsh marine environment and the limited food supply around breeding colonies. Each breeding attempt yields a clutch of two eggs [N_R_i = Each breeding attempt yields a clutch of two eggs], which is the maximum number of offspring a female can produce in a single nesting event. This fixed clutch size, unusual among birds where larger clutches might confer a selective advantage, reflects the high energetic cost of raising both a clutch and the semi-precocial young thereafter. Coupled with the fact that a breeding pair typically raises only one successful brood per year [F_R_i = one successful brood per year], the annual reproductive rate is effectively two offspring per year. This low annual fecundity is a hallmark of a slow life history, typical of many long-lived seabirds. The constraints on reproduction are further exacerbated by the risks of egg predation, inclement weather, and food shortages, meaning that many pairs may not even attempt to breed in poor years. The incubation period itself, during which the parents take turns maintaining the eggs at a stable temperature, is a demanding phase. Eggs are typically incubated at a constant 36 °C [T = 36 °C] to ensure optimal embryonic development, hatching after approximately 29 days [ab = approximately 29 days], a temperature that is maintained through close brooding and the development of a prominent brood patch by both parents.

Laying such a small clutch may seem counterintuitive for a species that can live for approximately 16 years, but it is a finely tuned strategy. The high survival of adults, coupled with a low but steady annual recruitment from the 2 eggs per clutch [N_R_i = 2 eggs per clutch] yielded annually, allows the population to remain stable without exhausting local prey resources. To complete a single successful breeding attempt, each parent must invest heavily in provisioning the two chicks. The ultimate body mass of an adult Great skua, a large, robust bird built for extended flight and aggressive piracy, is around 1340 grams [Wwi = around 1340 grams]. This considerable mass is supported by a diet rich in fish, eggs, and chicks of other birds, and provides the energy reserves necessary for long-distance migration within the North Atlantic. The combination of delayed reproduction, low annual fecundity, and substantial adult body size positions the Great skua as a textbook example of a K-selected, or slow, life-history strategy adapted to a stable but resource-poor environment.
